summary: Reviews integrity, privacy, and security issues when applying the Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) framework to SMTP. Earlier OPES work focused on HTTP, and data flows differently in email. The memo checks existing requirements for fit. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Letting helpers change things in transit works one way for web pages and another way for mail. This note checks what could go wrong for email.

questions: how do encrypted messages work with opes
subtitle: Applying Open Pluggable Edge Services to email and SMTP gateways.

tldr.problem: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) was designed for HTTP but is being adapted for SMTP email. Email data flows differently than HTTP, so existing OPES requirements need review for safety and effectiveness.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes how the OPES framework and IAB requirements map to SMTP, examining tracing, bypass mechanisms, and cryptographic compatibility, and proposes specific requirements for OPES/SMTP deployments.
tldr.outcome: OPES can standardize email gateway filtering and improve visibility and control, but it cannot guarantee reliable email delivery or fully protect end-to-end encrypted messages without sharing decryption keys.

facts.label: IAB considerations reviewed
facts.value: 7 (consent, IP addressing, notification, privacy, encryption, address rewriting)

today: RFC 4902 remains an important document for understanding the challenges of applying OPES to email. While the OPES working group eventually shut down without producing a full OPES/SMTP specification, email gateway filtering continues to be deployed widely. The document's analysis of tracing, bypass, and cryptographic compatibility issues remains relevant to any standardization effort in this space.

sections.title: Overview of OPES and Email Challenges
sections.content:
Open Pluggable Edge Services is a framework that allows intermediaries (edge services) to transform data on behalf of end users as it flows through the network. The framework was designed with HTTP in mind, where a client sends a request and the server responds within a single transaction.

Email and SMTP differ fundamentally. In HTTP, the end user (client) actively initiates the transaction and can specify preferences to intermediaries. In SMTP, mail flows unidirectionally from sender to recipients without a prior request from the recipients. This means the email recipient cannot directly request in-band that an OPES system bypass its processing, and OPES systems must add transparency mechanisms so recipients learn what has been modified.

Many email filters already operate at SMTP gateways today, often in non-standardized ways. OPES provides an opportunity to standardize these operations and address integrity, privacy, and security concerns, but with important limitations compared to HTTP deployments.
sections.eli5: OPES was built for web pages: you ask for something, a helper changes it, you get it. Email is different: someone sends you a message without asking, and a helper in the middle might change it. Email systems need different rules.

sections.title: Tracing and Visibility Mechanisms
sections.content:
When OPES systems process email, they must add tracing information so senders and recipients can identify which OPES services handled the message. Unlike HTTP headers, which many browsers do not display, email headers are typically visible to end users, providing good visibility into OPES processing.

The RFC requires that OPES systems add tracing headers (following SMTP conventions for "Received" headers or new headers like "OPES-System" and "OPES-Via") before calling any filtering or modification services. If a message cannot be delivered, the resulting Non-Delivery Report (NDR) must include OPES tracing information so the sender knows where the message was blocked.

Tracing enables recipients to detect compromised or misconfigured OPES systems and allows the chain of filtering to be audited. However, tracing information alone cannot prevent an OPES system from breaking a message in ways that make the tracing unreadable.
sections.eli5: When a helper changes your email, they must sign their name. If something goes wrong, the sender gets told which helper broke it. That way, you can find the problem.

sections.title: Bypass and Cryptographic Compatibility
sections.content:
The original OPES framework allows the data consumer (the recipient, in HTTP terms) to request that OPES bypass its processing by adding information to the request. In email, the recipient cannot make in-band bypass requests in the original message flow. Instead, if an email is blocked or broken by an OPES system, the recipient can contact the sender out-of-band (via separate email, web interface, or quarantine release mechanism) and ask them to resend with a bypass request.

Not all OPES services can be bypassed. Security-critical services like malware scanning should be mandatory, while transformations like language translation could be bypassed at the recipient's request.

Encrypted email messages present a fundamental challenge: OPES systems cannot inspect the content of encrypted messages unless given the decryption key. Sharing decryption keys with OPES intermediaries raises security and trust concerns. Message authentication using public-key signatures also presents difficulties: OPES systems cannot modify encrypted content and maintain end-to-end authentication without either sharing the sender's signing key (impractical) or re-signing modified content (requiring the recipient to trust both the original sender and the OPES system).
sections.eli5: If you want a helper to skip processing, you have to ask the sender to ask them—there is no shortcut. Encrypted mail is especially tricky: the helper cannot read it unless you give them your key, and if they change it, nobody can prove the sender sent that version.

sections.title: Protocol Requirements for OPES/SMTP
sections.content:
Based on the analysis, the RFC specifies four key requirements for OPES/SMTP protocols:

First, OPES systems MUST add tracing headers to email messages processed by the system. Second, if a message accepted by an OPES system cannot be delivered, the NDR MUST include OPES tracing information. Third, OPES/SMTP specifications MUST define a bypass request option that can be included in mail message headers, allowing the sender to indicate that certain OPES services should not process the message. Fourth, OPES/SMTP must define bypass request options as SMTP extension commands, allowing bypass requests within the SMTP dialog for operations that occur before the message body is transmitted.

These requirements distinguish OPES/SMTP from the original OPES/HTTP framework and address the fundamental differences in how email flows through networks compared to web requests.
sections.eli5: New rules for email systems: sign your work with a header. Tell senders if delivery failed. Let senders say 'skip this filter.' And let them say it in the SMTP conversation, too.

sections.title: Applying IAB Considerations to OPES/SMTP
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) established considerations for OPES that guide protocol and architecture design. The RFC reviews each consideration in the email context:

Consent: OPES operations must be authorized by either the sender or recipient. The OPES framework requires this, though non-compliant systems may ignore it. Notification: Senders must be able to detect and respond to recipient-centric OPES actions they deem inappropriate. Email headers provide visibility, but NDRs cannot guarantee that senders are notified of blocking. Non-blocking: If a non-OPES version of a message exists, OPES must not prevent users from receiving it. Bypass mechanisms address this. Privacy: OPES systems must support mechanisms for end users to determine the privacy policies of OPES intermediaries. Tracing information may raise additional privacy concerns that must be addressed.

Address rewriting and reference validity considerations apply less directly to email than to web protocols, since email addresses are simpler than URIs. However, OPES services that map internal addresses to external addresses must consistently update all affected email headers.
sections.eli5: The IAB said OPES must get permission, let people know what happened, let them opt out, and respect privacy. This note checks if email systems can do all that. Some are easy, some are hard.
